=== 58777 Steering Committee Cities Served by Oncor & Texas Coalition for Affordable Power Comments.pdf ===
                                           PROJECT NO. 58777

TRIENNIAL RELIABILITY                                §           BEFORE THE
ASSESSMENT FOR THE ERCOT                             §   PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
REGION UNDER § 25.508                                §            OF TEXAS

        STEERING COMMITTEE OF CITIES SERVED BY ONCOR AND TEXAS
        COALITION FOR AFFORDABLE POWER’S COMMENTS ON ERCOT’S
       PROPOSED ASSUMPTIONS FOR THE 2026 RELIABILITY ASSESSMENT

        The Steering Committee of Cities Served by Oncor (OCSC) and Texas Coalition for

Affordable Power (TCAP) (collectively, Cities) submit these comments (Comments) in response

to the Staff (Staff) of the Public Utility of Commission of Texas’ (Commission) January 30, 2026,

Questions for Comment on the Electric Reliability Council of Texas’ (ERCOT) Proposed

Assumptions for the 2026 Reliability Assessment.1 Commission Staff requested comments by

March 2, 2026. Therefore, these Comments are timely filed.

                                      I.     INTRODUCTION

        OCSC and TCAP are groups of over 170 municipalities and political subdivisions that

serve a unique stakeholder role. Cities rely on a competitive energy market for cost effective and

reliable power. In one capacity, Cities are power consumers that purchase electricity for various

uses, such as police, public buildings, water and wastewater, street lighting, and emergency

coordination. Public funds finance these functions—Cities, as stewards of these funds, thus have

an interest in competitive electricity costs. Cities also provide emergency services critical to the

health and safety of their citizens. Because a reliable grid supports these emergency services,

Cities support cost-effective policy that enhances reliability. OCSC and TCAP, therefore, have an

interest in the concepts at issue in this project.




        1
             Questions for Comment on ERCOT’s Proposed Assumptions for the 2026 Reliability Assessment
(Jan. 30, 2026).


                                                     1
                                II.   EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

       As requested, Cities have provided a one-page Executive Summary at the end of this

submission.

                     III.    RESPONSES TO STAFF’S QUESTIONS

       Below, Cities offer responses to Questions 1, 2, 3, and 8. At this time, Cities do not offer

responses to the remaining questions.

1. At the July 25, 2024 Open Meeting, the Commission approved setting the CONE at

   $140,000/MW-year for planning purposes in the ERCOT region, including the triennial

   reliability assessment. Based on stakeholder feedback, ERCOT has proposed a plan for

   updating this CONE value.

       a. Does CONE need to be updated for the 2026 reliability standard assessment?

             Why or why not?

       Cities do not believe that the Cost of New Entry (CONE) needs to be updated for the 2026

Reliability Assessment. As referenced above, three stakeholders in response to an ERCOT Market

Notice stated that the $140,000 per megawatt (MW)-year CONE value is out of date and should

be updated for the 2026 Reliability Assessment.2 On January 15, 2026, ERCOT recommended

that a truncated study be performed to identify an updated CONE value for use in the 2026

Reliability Assessment.3

       While Cities support having an accurate CONE value, performing an expedited CONE

study is unnecessary under these circumstances. CONE is an estimated, theoretical value for the

first-year net revenues that a representative resource must earn for a developer to be willing to



          2
            ERCOT Proposal to Update Cost of New Entry (CONE) for the 2026 Reliability Assessment at 2
(Jan. 15, 2026).
       3
           Id.


                                                  2
 build a generation investment in the ERCOT market. It is not the actual cost for a developer to

build generation, as costs will differ depending on the particular circumstances surrounding the

development. Thus, updating the CONE value for the 2026 Reliability Assessment on an

expedited timeline is not necessary. Cities recommend that ERCOT continue to use the 2024

CONE value when conducting the 2026 Reliability Assessment and that a full CONE study be

performed on a timeline separate from that of the 2026 Reliability Assessment.

       b. If the Commission considers an updated CONE value, are the scope and list of

           tasks proposed by Brattle and Sargent & Lundy in ERCOT’s January 15, 2026,

           filing an acceptable method to update the calculations? If not, please provide

           recommended modifications to their approach.

       If the Commission determines that an updated CONE value is necessary for the 2026

Reliability Assessment, updates to the calculations should be based on actual data rather than

assumptions. More specifically, when identifying technologies to be built for 2029 in the ERCOT

market and assessing associated costs, Brattle and Sargent & Lundy should focus their analyses

on actual data currently applicable to the ERCOT market. Thus, the CONE study should assess

the technologies that are most likely to be constructed in ERCOT, including solar and battery

energy storage. Focusing analyses on actual data that is currently pertinent to the ERCOT market

will ensure transparency and that any updates to the CONE value are accurate. Relying too heavily

on assumptions may lead to a higher or lower CONE value that would be even less representative

of the costs to build a generation investment in the ERCOT market than it otherwise would be.

2. ERCOT has requested the Commission consider whether the load forecasts used in this

   study should align with the one that will be generated through the 2026 RTP compliance

   plan described in the Commission’s rulemaking in Project No. 58480.                  ERCOT




                                               3
     acknowledges that an updated load forecast that aligns with that compliance plan could

    be ready by April or May 2026, which would push back the timeline of the reliability

    assessment by at least a month.

        a. Should the Commission approve updating the load forecast used in the 2026

              reliability assessment to align with the compliance plan being considered in

              Project No. 58480, even if it will delay work on the reliability assessment?

        Cities do not support updating the load forecast used in the 2026 Reliability Assessment to

align with the compliance plan being considered in Project No. 58480 if this will result in any

delays to the 2026 Reliability Assessment. Cities emphasize the importance of accurate load

forecasting, considering the influx of large load customers which are being added in abundance to

the ERCOT system. However, ERCOT has stated it anticipates the load forecast based on the

2026 Regional Transmission Plan (RTP) compliance plan could be ready in April or May of 2026.4

While it could be beneficial to use the updated load forecast in the 2026 Reliability Assessment,

Cities are concerned that stakeholders and the Commission will not have ample time to review the

2026 Reliability Assessment if an updated load forecast were to be used. Consequently, Cities

conclude that that the load forecasts used in the 2026 Reliability Assessment do not necessarily

have to align with the ones with the 2026 RTP Compliance Plan.5                          Instead, ERCOT and

stakeholders can assess how an updated forecast would impact the 2026 Reliability Assessment

without delaying the assessment itself.

        b. What other considerations should the Commission make regarding the load

              forecast used for the 2026 and 2029 simulation years?



        4
            ERCOT’s Initial Proposed Modeling Assumptions for the 2026 Reliability Assessment at 4 (Jan. 15, 2026).
        5
          See Rulemaking to Establish Large Load Forecasting Criteria PURA § 37.0561, Project No. 58480, Order
Adopting New § 25.370 (Feb. 6, 2026).


                                                         4
         Cities again caution against the use of large load forecasts which are likely overstated. On

August 9, 2024, Cities provided comments relating to ERCOT’s Reliability Plan for the Permian

Basin.6 Cities noted in those comments the potential for stranded transmission costs due to highly

speculative load forecasts anticipated in the Permian Basin.7 Cities also stressed the need to

validate these load forecasts, considering neither the Commission nor ERCOT validated the

forecasts provided by Transmission and Distribution Service Providers (TDSP) relating to the

projected load in the Permian Basin.8 Similarly, on October 17, 2025, Cities argued that ERCOT’s

large load forecasts may be overstated, considering ERCOT forecasted that energy demand would

reach 145 gigawatts by 2031.9           Cities emphasized stakeholder involvement when making

adjustments to a TDSP’s load data for purposes of large load forecasting criteria since ERCOT

unilaterally adjusted 2025 TDSP-provided large load forecasts using methodology changes that

were not based on collaboration with stakeholders.10 The 89th Texas Legislature enacted Senate

Bill (SB) 6 in part to promote more accurate load forecasts and establish specific criteria by which

ERCOT includes forecasted large load in its transmission planning and resource adequacy models

and reports.11 Considering the importance of the 2026 Reliability Assessment and the fact that the

load forecasts are speculative, Cities urge the Commission to allow for stakeholder input when

assessing the load forecasts used for the 2026 and 2029 simulation years.




         6
           See Reliability Plan for the Permian Basin Under PURA § 39.167, Project No. 55718, Comments of the
Steering Committee of Cities Served by Oncor and Texas Coalition for Affordable Power at 1-2 (Aug. 9, 2024).
        7
             Id.
        8
             Id. at 3.
        9
            Project No. 58480, OCSC and TCAP’s Comments on Proposed Large Load Forecasting Criteria at 1-2
(Oct. 17, 2025).
        10
             Id. at 3.
        11
             Id. at 2.

 3. ERCOT proposed using the December 2025 Capacity, Demand, and Reserves (CDR)

    Report to create the base portfolio for evaluating the bulk power system in 2026 and

    2029. This includes resource additions and retirements.

        a. Does the generation portfolio in the December 2025 CDR Report adequately

             capture the resource mix in both 2026 and 2029?                       If not, what additional

             assumptions should be made about resource additions and retirements?

        The generation portfolio in the December 2025 CDR Report is an important input in

determining resources that are necessary to meet the projected decline in the reserve margin, but

it should be noted that the CDR Report generally includes a conservative generation forecast.

Thus, the generation portfolio in the December 2025 CDR Report will likely not resemble the

actual load which materializes over the next five summer and winter peak seasons. This is because

markets will adjust over time to information on scarcity, and new information on data inputs will

come to light which the CDR Report methodology does not take into account. Additionally,

ERCOT dictates that a planned resource can only be included in the CDR Report if the resource

has signed a Standard Generation Interconnection Agreement and posted financial security.12

Excluding proposed generation investments which do not yet meet ERCOT’s requirements results

in underestimating likely future capacity.

        Moreover, the December 2025 CDR Report reflects a large amount of uncertainty,

considering it includes three alternative Planning Reserve Margin scenarios which produce very

different spreads of reserve margin outcomes. Scenario 1 in the December 2025 CDR Report

applies the SB 6 provision that new data centers must be curtailable in an energy emergency to




        12
                  ERCOT      Current     Planning    Guide,        Section    6:     Data/Modeling   at   6.9(1),
https://www.ercot.com/mktrules/guides/planning/current (last visited Feb. 25, 2026).


                                                        6
 ERCOT’s base case. Scenario 2 and 3 apply varying impacts to the projected reserve margin. For

2030, the three scenarios produce a spread of reserve margin outcomes as wide as (12.7 percent)

to 35 percent. While the CDR Report is an important tool for assessing the Resource Adequacy

in the ERCOT region, the uncertainties surrounding the path of both load resource expansion and

whether ERCOT can indeed curtail data center loads render the CDR Report much more uncertain

than in the past. Thus, Cities urge that these uncertainties surrounding the December CDR Report

be considered if it is used to create the base portfolio for evaluating the bulk power system in 2026

and 2029.

8. ERCOT proposed modifying how the model accounts for the effectiveness of the

   Commission's weatherization rule 16 TAC § 25.55. Previously, it was estimated to reduce

   weather-related outages by 85%, however under ERCOT' s proposed approach, the

   rule’s effectiveness would decline during extreme temperatures.

       a. Do you agree with ERCOT's recommendation to deviate from the 85%

             effectiveness for the weatherization rule?

       Cities do not agree with ERCOT’s recommendation to deviate from the 85% effectiveness

for the weatherization rule. 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.55 provides winter and summer preparation

measures that a generation entity must complete for each resource under its control.13 While

ERCOT is recommending to decrease the rule’s effectiveness for purposes of the 2026 Reliability

Assessment, ERCOT has completed at least 450 weatherization inspections during this winter

season and reported that it successfully managed the grid during Winter Storm Fern, despite a

period of extreme cold and freezing precipitation.14 Considering these recent performance results,



       13
            16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.55.
       14
            ERCOT, Post-Event Report – Winter Storm Fern – January 2026 (Jan. 28, 2026),
https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/01/28/ERCOT-Post-Event-Report-Winter-Storm-Fern.pdf.


                                                 7
 decreasing the 85% effectiveness for the weatherization rule seems unnecessary and could lead to

inaccuracies in the 2026 Reliability Assessment. Cities, thus, recommend that the assumed

effectiveness of the Commission’s weatherization rule remain 85% until there is evidence to

support the contrary.

                                   IV.    CONCLUSION

       Cities appreciate the opportunity to provide comments on ERCOT’s proposed assumptions

for the 2026 Reliability Assessment. Cities look forward to working with the Commission and

stakeholders on developing the first triennial assessment of the Commission’s reliability standard.


Date: March 2, 2026

        2026 Reliability Assessment on an expedited timeline is not necessary.

        than assumptions.

•       The CONE study should assess the technologies that are most likely to be constructed in

        ERCOT, including solar and battery energy storage.

•       Cities do not support updating the load forecast used in the 2026 Reliability Assessment to

                  Reliability Assessment if an updated load forecast were to be used.

•       Cities caution against the use of large load forecasts which are likely overstated and urge

        the Commission to allow for stakeholder input when assessing the load forecasts used for

        the 2026 and 2029 simulation years.

•       The generation portfolio in the December 2025 CDR Report will likely not resemble the

        uncertainty.

•       Cities recommend that the assumed effectiveness of the Commission’s weatherization rule

        remain 85% until there is evidence to support the contrary.
